title: To Victory
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 39 of 40
content:
Danse stopped saying Ad Victoriam for almost four months.

I noticed because he used to say it constantly.

Before missions. After briefings. As greeting, farewell, encouragement, punctuation.

After banishment, the phrase vanished.

I never asked why.

Then one morning, settlers arrived at our house asking for help.

A group of raiders had taken the bridge north of their farms. Not a Brotherhood concern. Not strategic technology. No elder had issued an order.

Just people in danger.

Danse picked up his rifle.

“Let’s go.”

The fight was difficult.

The raiders had fortified the bridge with mines and firing positions. Danse studied the approach, planned routes, assigned civilians who insisted on helping to safe positions, and then looked at me.

“Ready?”

“Always.”

“That’s objectively false.”

“Romantic.”

He smiled.

We moved.

The battle felt different from Brotherhood operations only because nobody above us would write a report.

Danse was still Danse.

He called targets. Protected flanks. Shouted at one settler for exposing himself. Took a round against his armor and kept moving.

I was still me.

I argued with a tactical instruction in the middle of gunfire.

He yelled that we would discuss it later.

We won.

Not cleanly. One settler took a bullet through the leg. A section of bridge collapsed. My coat caught fire briefly, which Danse found much less funny than I did.

But the raiders fled.

The road reopened.

As the settlers carried the wounded home, Danse stood on the bridge watching them go.

I moved beside him.

“Objective complete?”

He looked at me.

“Yes.”

“Successful thing?”

His smile appeared.

“Yes.”

The wind moved over the river.

Danse stared toward the settlement.

“Ad Victoriam,” he said.

I turned.

He seemed surprised by the words too.

“I thought you were done with that.”

“So did I.”

“What changed?”

Danse considered.

“I used to think victory meant the Brotherhood’s objective survived.”

“And now?”

“The people did.”

Simple.

Enough.

I took his hand.

“To victory,” I said.

His fingers closed around mine.

We walked home beneath a clear sky.

That night we ate too much, drank beer on the porch, and listened to Danse play six entire chords badly enough that the dog from the neighboring farm left.

“You’re improving,” I lied.

“My transitions are cleaner.”

“The dog disagrees.”

“The dog has no musical training.”

“Neither do you.”

Danse set the guitar aside.

“Come here.”

“That sounded like an order.”

“It was.”

“I thought we established—”

He pulled me into his lap and kissed me.

I forgot the argument.

Later, the lantern burned low in the bedroom.

Danse sat beside me with the confidence that had grown slowly between us, always pausing long enough to make choice visible. I answered by leaning into him. We kissed until the argument had become a joke again, then let the kiss end without forcing it to become anything else.

We lay tangled beneath the blankets while rain began outside.

Danse traced one finger along my hand.

“Do you regret it?” he asked.

“What?”

“Choosing me.”

I turned toward him.

“No.”

“Even knowing what I am?”

“Especially knowing who you are.”

He closed his eyes.

The difference between what and who had once seemed impossible to him.

Now he breathed through it.

“Ad Victoriam,” I whispered.

Danse smiled in the dark.

“Ad Victoriam.”

The bridge fight brought visitors for days.

Settlers arrived with food, ammunition, spare lumber, and gratitude Danse did not know what to do with.

He tried to refuse everything.

Mara ignored him and put two jars of preserved vegetables on our kitchen shelf.

The workshop owner left a replacement set of guitar strings.

A farmer delivered a bag of coffee beans and said, “Maybe whoever makes yours can save you.”

I nearly collapsed laughing.

Danse stood in the doorway holding the beans like evidence in a murder case.

“My coffee is not that bad.”

The farmer had already left.

“It has become a regional issue,” I told him.

“This is slander.”

“Public health concern.”

He pointed the bag at me.

“You encouraged this.”

“Ad Victoriam.”

The expression that crossed his face stopped me.

Not pain exactly.

Surprise at hearing the words in our kitchen.

I set the joke aside.

“Too much?”

“No.”

Danse placed the beans on the counter.

“I’m trying to understand why it felt different on the bridge.”

“You told me. The people survived.”

“That’s part of it.”

He leaned against the counter.

“When I said it before, victory was always attached to a larger campaign. Recover the technology. destroy the target. secure the area. advance the Brotherhood.”

“And now?”

“Now I think victory can be smaller.”

He looked around the house.

“A repaired pump. A road people can use. Lena staying where she chose. Three chords.”

“Four.”

“Four.”

I smiled.

“Coffee not killing anyone.”

“That has never occurred.”

“Debatable.”

He came closer.

“Do you know why I kept the phrase?”

“You like Latin?”

“I don’t speak Latin.”

“That has never stopped anybody.”

He shook his head.

“Because it reminded me that survival was supposed to lead somewhere.”

The humor left me.

Danse rested his hands on my hips.

“For a while after Bravo, I thought surviving Maxson’s order was the end of something. Maybe it was.”

He looked toward the workshop window.

“But I did not know there could be another direction afterward.”

“To whatever comes next.”

He nodded.

“That.”

A knock interrupted us.

Rhys stood on the porch.

For one terrifying second neither Danse nor I moved.

Rhys wore civilian clothes beneath a Brotherhood jacket with the insignia covered by a strip of cloth. No power armor. No escort.

Danse’s face went empty.

“Knight Rhys.”

Rhys winced.

“Don’t.”

Danse’s hands dropped from me.

“What are you doing here?”

“Haylen sent this.”

He held out a sealed packet.

Danse did not take it.

Rhys looked at me.

I stayed out of reach of the decision.

Finally Danse accepted the packet.

“Is she safe?”

“Yes.”

“Are you?”

Rhys shrugged.

“Depends who you ask.”

That was so Rhys I nearly laughed.

Danse’s mouth moved too.

Neither man seemed to know what to do next.

So Rhys did what soldiers do when emotion becomes unbearable.

He inspected the porch railing.

“This brace is wrong.”

Danse’s head snapped toward it.

“It is not.”

“Angle’s off.”

“It has held through three storms.”

“Still wrong.”

Five minutes later they were arguing over carpentry like nothing had happened.

It was not nothing.

That was why it worked.

Rhys stayed for dinner.

He did not apologize for the Brotherhood. Danse did not ask him to. They talked about Haylen, the Gladius dead, the Prydwen, new recruits, a scribe who had accidentally dropped a wrench through a maintenance grate and shut down half a deck.

Danse listened like a starving man trying not to eat too fast.

When Rhys left, he stood at the bottom of the porch steps.

“I don’t know what I’m supposed to call you.”

Danse looked at him.

“Danse.”

Rhys nodded.

“Right.”

He hesitated.

“Ad Victoriam.”

Danse’s eyes closed for half a second.

Then he answered.

“Ad Victoriam.”

Rhys walked away.

Danse remained on the porch holding Haylen’s packet.

Inside was a letter, four pages in her cramped handwriting, and Keane’s old baseball card from the casualty wall in Cambridge.

Danse sat down hard.

I sat beside him.

He read the letter twice.

Then pressed the card against his mouth and cried quietly.

Not from despair.

Not entirely from grief.

From connection surviving a border he thought had become absolute.

When he could speak, he looked at me.

“She doesn’t regret knowing me.”

I remembered the unsent letter at Bravo.

“No.”

“She said she’s furious.”

I smiled.

“Of course she did.”

Danse laughed through tears.

Haylen’s letter contained no grand declaration.

That made it more painful.

She complained about Rhys. Described a new scribe who mislabeled half the station’s medical supplies. Told Danse the old transmitter still cut out whenever it rained. Wrote that Maxson had not rescinded the order barring him from Brotherhood facilities and that she was not stupid enough to test it.

Then, near the end, one line made Danse stop breathing for a second.

*Cambridge still feels like your station sometimes.*

He handed me the page because his hands had started shaking.

I read it twice.

“She misses you.”

“Yes.”

“She’s angry.”

“Yes.”

“She sent you Keane’s card.”

Danse looked down at the battered piece of cardboard.

“She remembered.”

Of course she had.

The dead on the roster had belonged to all of them.

So had the living.

Danse folded Haylen’s letter along the original creases.

“Do you want to answer?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“Tonight?”

“No.”

A few months ago he would have treated delay like failure.

Now he set the paper beside the lamp.

“Tomorrow,” he said.

“Good.”

He looked at me.

“I’m learning that word.”

“Tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

The future had become something he could schedule without needing permission to have it.

That night, before bed, he placed Keane’s card beneath the old holotag in the workshop.

Then he looked at the words over the bench.

DANSE.

“Ad Victoriam,” he said softly.

Not to the Brotherhood.

Not away from it either.

To the life that kept becoming larger than the rules he had inherited.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
